title: Injection / Input Validation
summary: Untrusted input flows into a query, command, path, or template without being separated from the instruction. A crafted value then changes what the code executes. The fix is almost always to pass the value as data (a bound parameter, an argv list, a safe join) rather than concatenating it into a string.
example_bad:
q = f"SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = '{email}'"
db.execute(q)

videos.title: Running an SQL Injection Attack - Computerphile

micro_check.prompt: Which change most reliably prevents SQL injection?
options: Escaping quote characters in the input string
Using a parameterised query with bound values
Rejecting inputs longer than 100 characters
Running the query as a low-privilege database user
micro_check.explanation: Bound parameters keep the value as data, so it can never be parsed as SQL. Escaping and length limits are bypassable; least privilege only limits the blast radius.

micro_check.prompt: Code builds a shell command by concatenating a user-supplied hostname and runs it through the shell. The safest fix is to:
options: Wrap the call in try/except
Strip semicolons and backticks from the hostname
Run the command via an argument list with the shell disabled
Log the command before running it
micro_check.explanation: Passing an argv list with the shell disabled means the OS never interprets shell metacharacters. Blocklisting characters is a losing game.

micro_check.prompt: During review, which pattern is the red flag for an injection defect?
options: A value read from an environment variable
A hard-coded constant used in a query
A user-supplied value concatenated into a query/command/path string
A value checked against an allowlist before use
micro_check.explanation: Injection is untrusted input reaching an interpreter without separation. Concatenating a user value into an instruction string is the classic shape.

title: Auth & Access Control
summary: The code authenticates a user but never checks that this user is allowed to touch this resource. Any logged-in caller can act on another user's data by changing an id (IDOR), or a role check is written so it always passes. The fix is an explicit ownership or permission check against the current user before the action.

videos.title: Broken Access Control - OWASP Top 10 (F5 DevCentral)
Insecure Direct Object Reference (IDOR) Explained - PwnFunction

micro_check.prompt: An endpoint loads a record by an id from the URL but never checks who owns it. This is:
options: A SQL injection
An IDOR / broken access control bug
A race condition
A resource leak
micro_check.explanation: Authenticated but not authorised: any logged-in user can read another user's data by changing the id. Add an ownership check.

micro_check.prompt: The correct fix for the IDOR in get_invoice(invoice_id) is to:
options: Hash the invoice_id in the URL so it can't be guessed
Add Invoice.user_id == current_user.id to the query
Rate-limit the endpoint
Return 404 instead of 403
micro_check.explanation: Scope the query to the current user so a foreign id simply returns nothing. Obscuring the id is not access control.

micro_check.prompt: Why is `if user.role != 'admin' or True:` inside a permission check a defect?
options: It is slower than a direct comparison
role should be an enum, not a string
The `or True` makes the condition always pass, so the guard is dead
It should use `and` instead of `or`
micro_check.explanation: The condition can never be false, so the check can never deny. A permission guard must actually be able to reject.

title: Error & Exception Handling
summary: A failure is swallowed instead of handled. A bare except that does nothing, a return value that is never checked, or an error path that leaves the object half-built. The caller then proceeds on bad data and fails later with a confusing message. The fix is to catch the specific error, act on it, and signal failure clearly.

videos.title: Using Try/Except Blocks for Error Handling - Corey Schafer

micro_check.prompt: Why is `try: ... except Exception: pass` a problem?
options: It is slower than letting the error propagate
It swallows the failure, so the caller proceeds on bad or missing data
`Exception` should be `BaseException`
`pass` is not valid inside an except block
micro_check.explanation: Silently discarding the error hides the failure; downstream code then fails later with a confusing symptom. Catch a specific exception and act on it.

micro_check.prompt: You catch an exception you cannot fully handle. Best practice is to:
options: Catch the specific type, then re-raise or signal failure clearly
Catch bare Exception and return None
Catch bare Exception and print it
Avoid try/except entirely
micro_check.explanation: Narrow the catch and keep the failure visible: re-raise, return an explicit error result, or wrap it in a domain exception.

micro_check.prompt: A function returns None on failure and the caller never checks the return value. This is:
options: Fine, since None is falsy
A concurrency bug
An unchecked-error defect: the caller acts on a missing value
Only a style issue
micro_check.explanation: An error path that isn't checked is the same class of bug as a swallowed exception: the program continues on invalid state.

title: Concurrency & State
summary: Two things run at once and step on shared state. A check-then-act gap where another thread slips in between, a counter updated without a lock, or a default argument shared across calls. The bug is timing-dependent and hard to reproduce. The fix is to make the read-modify-write atomic, or to not share the state at all.
example_bad:
if key not in cache:
    cache[key] = factory()

videos.title: Clarifying the Issues with Mutable Default Arguments - Corey Schafer

micro_check.prompt: `if key not in cache: cache[key] = compute()` run by multiple threads can:
options: Leak memory
Compute the value twice or corrupt the dict, due to a check-then-act race
Raise SyntaxError
Deadlock immediately
micro_check.explanation: Another thread can slip between the check and the assignment. Make the read-modify-write atomic with a lock, or use a thread-safe structure.

micro_check.prompt: Why is `def add(x, items=[]):` that appends to items buggy?
options: Lists cannot be default arguments
It should be written as items=list()
The default list is created once and shared across all calls
append is not thread-safe
micro_check.explanation: The default is evaluated once at definition time; every call with no argument mutates the same list. Use items=None and create it inside.

micro_check.prompt: Most reliable fix for a counter incremented by many threads without a lock:
options: Make the counter a float
Add a short sleep before each update
Guard the update with a lock, or use an atomic primitive
Use a larger integer type
micro_check.explanation: `n += 1` is read-modify-write and not atomic. A lock (or an atomic counter) makes the update safe.

title: Logic & Boundary
summary: The code runs but computes the wrong thing. An off-by-one in a loop bound, a comparison that should be >= not >, a condition that is inverted, or the wrong branch returned. No crash, just quietly wrong output. The fix is to trace the boundary and edge cases by hand.
example_bad:
for i in range(len(arr)):
    if arr[i] == arr[i + 1]:  # IndexError on the last i
example_good:
for i in range(len(arr) - 1):
    if arr[i] == arr[i + 1]:

videos.title: Bounds Checking & Off-by-One Errors in Arrays

micro_check.prompt: `for i in range(len(arr)): if arr[i] == arr[i + 1]:` fails because:
options: range is exclusive of its end value
On the last i, arr[i + 1] is out of bounds
== should be `is`
The loop is O(n^2)
micro_check.explanation: The loop should stop at len(arr) - 1. Classic off-by-one / boundary defect: no crash until the final iteration.

micro_check.prompt: A boundary or logic bug typically shows up as:
options: An immediate crash on any input
Correct-looking runs that return subtly wrong results at the edges
A memory leak
A CORS error
micro_check.explanation: Logic and off-by-one bugs usually run fine and just compute the wrong thing. Trace the edge cases (0, 1, last element) by hand.

micro_check.prompt: Using `if age > 18:` to allow adults is likely wrong because:
options: age might be a string
18-year-olds are excluded; it should be >=
It should be elif
Integers cannot be compared with >
micro_check.explanation: Off-by-one on the comparison operator. Decide whether the boundary value is included and choose > vs >= deliberately.

title: Resource & Performance
summary: The code holds a resource it never releases, or does work that grows faster than the input. A connection opened per loop and never closed, a cache that grows forever, or an O(n) membership test inside an O(n) loop. It works on small inputs and falls over on real ones. The fix is a context manager, a bound, or a better data structure.

videos.title: Introduction to Big O Notation and Time Complexity - CS Dojo
Context Managers - Efficiently Managing Resources - Corey Schafer

micro_check.prompt: `if item not in out:` where out is a list, inside a loop over items, is slow because:
options: List membership is O(n), making the loop O(n^2)
Lists cannot hold duplicates
`in` copies the list each time
It allocates a new list each iteration
micro_check.explanation: Each `x in list` scans the whole list. Track seen values in a set for O(1) membership.

micro_check.prompt: Opening a database connection inside a loop and never closing it is a:
options: Logic bug
Resource leak: use a context manager or connection pool
Race condition
Injection risk
micro_check.explanation: Unreleased handles accumulate until the process runs out. Use `with` or a pool so each connection is returned.

micro_check.prompt: A cache backed by a plain dict that only ever grows will eventually:
options: Raise KeyError
Exhaust memory; it needs a size bound or eviction policy
Become read-only
Slow `in` down to O(n)
micro_check.explanation: An unbounded cache is a slow memory leak. Bound it with an LRU, a max size, or a TTL.
